title: The Effect of Crowding on Human Task Performance

findings.antecedent: high population density (small room: 35 sq ft, 5 or 9 subjects; moderate room: 80 sq ft, 5 or 9 subjects)
findings.consequent: performance on various tasks (group discussion, crossing-out, forming words, object uses, memory, concentration)
findings.p_value: not reported, stated as no significant effects
findings.mechanism: Density per se does not function as an ordinary aversive, arousing stimulus.
findings.source: Results and Discussion, page 12, and Table 1
findings.quote: there were no effects of any kind attributable to the level of density in the rooms.

findings.mechanism: no indication that density produced greater effects over time.
findings.quote: none at the end, and none in terms of changes from beginning to end... no effects of density.

findings.p_value: not reported, stated as no differences

stimuli.description: rooms of 160, 80, and 35 square feet, with either nine or five subjects in each room. Subjects were seated on wooden chairs with desk-type arms.

limitations: The length of time during which subjects were crowded was only 4 hours, and subjects knew that it was limited. Effects might appear only with much greater duration or if subjects are unaware of eventual relief from crowding.
The experimental situation was relatively formal and structured, with specific tasks, limited verbal interactions, and subjects being strangers with no anticipation of a long-term relationship.

The activity did not involve much physical movement, so participants did not get in each other's way or interfere physically with each other's work, and did not have to use available space for moving around.
